newsitem.title: UK: UK may allow 44 tonne trucks on six axles in 1999.
newsitem.headline: UK may allow 44 tonne trucks on six axles in 1999.

text.p: British Rail and Roads Minister John Watts announced on Monday proposals for 44-tonne six-axle trucks, raising the UK weight limit from 38 tonnes, a move he said could cut road wear and lead to greater effiency.
"Forty-four tonne six-axle lorries cause no more wear to roads or bridges than the 38 tonne five-axle lorries allowed generally now," Watts told a news conference.
If approved, the new regulations would not come into force before 1999 and apply solely to trucks operating in so called "piggyback' road/rail operations, where the trailer is carried by rail.

An EU directive that member states must accept international trucks weighing up to 40 tonnes will come into force in Britain on January 1 1999, by which time bridges should have been assessed and strengthened where necessary.

Department of Transport sources said since Britain would be obliged to raise the weight threshold from 38 to 40 tonnes under the ruling, it would be more beneficial economically and environmentally to bring in 44 tonne/six-axle trucks.

Asked about the effect of the move on rail companies, Watts said: "The Government wishes to allow freight companies the opportunity to develop their businesses and capture new traffic. It also wishes to encourage piggyback road/rail operations."
He said the government would consider providing grants to help firms such as Railtrack finance the upgrading of bridges to cope with the extra weight.
"Railtrack will not be required to spend money," he said.
With the general election just months away and British voters reluctant to see heavy trucks pounding their roads, Watts said the heavier vehicles would be no larger or noisier than existing trucks.
They would also have to have the same stopping distance as 38 tonne trucks, the sources said.

Since 1994, certain types of lorry have been allowed to operate at up to 44 tonnes on combined road/rail routes, in a bid to encourage freight traffic through the Channel Tunnel. Department of Transport data showed this had attracted a significant proportion of heavy goods freight from roads.
Watts did not rule out the possible introduction of 44 tonne trucks into general transportation, but noted that this could eventually take market share away from the rail companies.
